answer: SkipGram does not directly operate on the Wikipedia word network as a graph algorithm; instead, it learns dense word embeddings from local word co-occurrence in text, and those embeddings implicitly capture the structure of the Wikipedia corpus. In practice, words that appear in similar contexts end up with vectors that encode semantic and syntactic regularities, so analogy tasks can be solved by simple vector arithmetic (for example, king - man + woman ≈ queen). This differs from graph-based methods, which typically use explicit edges and graph structure to propagate similarity or rank nodes. SkipGram’s analogy performance comes from the geometry of the learned embedding space rather than from traversing or optimizing over the word network itself.
